Elliptic differential equations are a class of partial differential equations (PDEs) that arise in various fields of __science__ and __engineering__.

Typically, they are used to model phenomena such as:

- Steady-state heat distribution
- Electrostatic potential
- Gravitational potential
- Fluid flow
- Elasticity
- ...
  


Assume you are given an [elliptic differential equaiton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_partial_differential_equation)
possibly of the form:

$$
\begin{cases}
- \Delta u(x,y) &= f(x,y) & \forall (x,y) \in \Omega \\
u(x,y) &= g(x,y) & \forall (x,y)/ \in \partial \Omega
\end{cases}
$$

on the region $Omega = (0,1)^2$. In this case, we would deal with a poisson
equation. And lets say, we wish to model gravity. In 3D, this would mean that
$\Delta u = 4 \pi \rho$, where $\rho$ is our mass density function. Because we
are dealing with 2D here, we will not use the area of a sphere, but instead
use the area of a disk, so we replace $4 \pi$ by $2 \pi$. The mass density would
assign each point in our space $\Omega$ the mass which is located there. An
example could be the one one I plotted here:

<iframe src="https://www.desmos.com/3d/dcevrb5isv" width="100%" style="min-height:300px"></iframe> 

This would represent two objects at points $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ of different
sizes and with different masses.
Or, similarily, we could imagine $\Omega$ hosting a point-cloud of
particles. $\rho$ would then represent the amount of particles in a small region
around a given point (i.e. their _mass_).

$$\Delta u(x,y) = \left(\frac{ \partial^2 }{ \partial x^2 }u(x,y)\right)^2 + \left(\frac{ \partial^2 }{ \partial y^2 }u(x,y)\right)^2$$

or equivalently:

$$
\Delta u(x,y) = \nabla \cdot \nabla u(x,y)
$$

where $\nabla u(x,y)$ is the gradient vector field, associating to each point
in $\Omega$ the vector of steepest ascent and $\nabla \cdot$ takes in a vector
field and measures for each point how much, for a small region the vectors flow
out of it (the divergence). Together, this means that $\Delta u$ measures the
net outflow of the gradient field for each point:

- Positive Laplacian: Means the "uphill" vectors are generally pointing out 
  from the point (like an upside-down cone, a minimum).
- Negative Laplacian: Means the "uphill" vectors are generally pointing in 
  toward the point (like a normal hill, a maximum).


So $- \Delta u(x,y) = f(x,y) \forall (x,y) \in \Omega$ means the higher $f(x,y)$ is,
the more negative $-\Delta u(x)$ is, and therefor more points near $(x,y)$ are
attracted to it. This is exactly what we would expect from gravitational force!
We may see this more clearly, be pushing the signs around: 
$\Delta u(x,y) = - f(x,y) \forall (x,y) \in \Omega$

It might be a good idea to also visualize our mirrored $f$:

<iframe src="https://www.desmos.com/3d/3jewa9gusw" width="100%" style="min-height:300px"></iframe> 

And this might look familiar to an experiment intended to explain gravity, which
I assume most have already seen:

<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/MTY1Kje0yLg?si=GYK5YN2Hgvft0cyZ" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

![example of the laplacian being negative or positive](assets/laplacian.png)

The influx in the above picture is represented by the laplacian $\Delta u$.
The gray space around the point $(x,y)$ would then be the other values which $u$
takes on in a neighborhood around $(x,y)$.

---

How can we find $u$ given the above poisson equation?

We will calculate the solution approximately on a grid

```{python}
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Parameters
N = 10
h = 1 / (N + 1)

# Unit square in (x,y) plane
square = ([0, 1, 1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1, 1, 0], [0]*5)

# Interior grid points (blue)
grid_x = [i*h for i in range(1, N+1) for j in range(1, N+1)]
grid_y = [j*h for i in range(1, N+1) for j in range(1, N+1)]
grid_z = [0] * len(grid_x)

# Boundary points (red)
boundary = [(x,y,z) 
  for (x,i) in [ (i*h,i) for i in range(N+2) ] 
  for (y,j) in [ (i*h,i) for i in range(N+2) ] 
  for z in [0]
  if i == 0 or j == 0 or i == N+1 or j == N+1
]

# Create figure
fig = go.Figure()

# Add unit square, interior grid points, and boundary points
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=square[0], y=square[1], z=square[2], mode='lines',
                           line=dict(color='black', width=4), name='Unit Square'))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=grid_x, y=grid_y, z=grid_z, mode='markers',
                           marker=dict(size=5, color='blue'), name=f'Interior (N={N})'))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(
  x=[v[0] for v in boundary],
  y=[v[1] for v in boundary],
  z=[v[2] for v in boundary],
  mode='markers',
  marker=dict(size=5, color='red'),
  name='Boundary'))

# Update layout
fig.update_layout(
    title=f'Unit Square in (x,y) Plane with Grid Points (N={N}, h={h:.4f})',
    scene=dict(xaxis_title='X', yaxis_title='Y', zaxis_title='Z', aspectmode='cube'),
    showlegend=True, width=800, height=800
)

fig.show()
```

## Finite differences — from scratch

The standard approach for numerically solving the Poisson equation on a
uniform grid is the **finite difference method**.  We replace the Laplacian
with its five-point stencil:

$$
-\Delta u(x_i, y_j) \approx \frac{4u_{i,j} - u_{i-1,j} - u_{i+1,j} - u_{i,j-1} - u_{i,j+1}}{h^2}
= f(x_i, y_j)
$$

where $h = \tfrac{1}{N+1}$ is the grid spacing and $(x_i, y_j) = (ih, jh)$
for $i,j \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ are the interior nodes.  Stacking all $N^2$
equations in row-major order gives a linear system $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{b}$.

The following implementation builds that system in a purely functional
style (no mutable loops, only `map`, list comprehensions, and `reduce`).

```{python}
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from functools import reduce

# ── problem parameters ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
N = 30              # interior grid points per axis
h = 1 / (N + 1)    # grid spacing

# ── source term: two Gaussian mass concentrations ─────────────────────────────
def f(x, y):
    rho1 = 3.0 * np.exp(-60 * ((x - 0.25)**2 + (y - 0.25)**2))
    rho2 = 1.5 * np.exp(-60 * ((x - 0.70)**2 + (y - 0.65)**2))
    return 2 * np.pi * (rho1 + rho2)

# ── grid coordinates (1-indexed, interior only) ────────────────────────────────
xs = list(map(lambda i: (i + 1) * h, range(N)))
ys = list(map(lambda j: (j + 1) * h, range(N)))

# ── flat index for interior node (i, j) ──────────────────────────────────────
def idx(i, j): return i * N + j

# ── generate all (row, col, value) stencil triplets functionally ──────────────
def stencil_entries(N, h):
    diag  = [(idx(i,j), idx(i,j),    4/h**2) for i in range(N) for j in range(N)]
    left  = [(idx(i,j), idx(i,j-1), -1/h**2) for i in range(N) for j in range(1, N)]
    right = [(idx(i,j), idx(i,j+1), -1/h**2) for i in range(N) for j in range(0, N-1)]
    up    = [(idx(i,j), idx(i-1,j), -1/h**2) for i in range(1, N) for j in range(N)]
    down  = [(idx(i,j), idx(i+1,j), -1/h**2) for i in range(0, N-1) for j in range(N)]
    return diag + left + right + up + down

# ── assemble dense matrix via reduce ─────────────────────────────────────────
def add_entry(A, entry):
    r, c, v = entry
    A[r, c] += v
    return A

A = reduce(add_entry,
           stencil_entries(N, h),
           np.zeros((N * N, N * N)))

# ── right-hand side ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
b = np.array([f(xs[i], ys[j]) for i in range(N) for j in range(N)])

# ── solve and reshape ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
U = np.linalg.solve(A, b).reshape(N, N)

# ── visualise ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
fig = go.Figure(data=[
    go.Surface(x=X, y=Y, z=U.T, colorscale='Viridis',
               contours=dict(z=dict(show=True, usecolormap=True, highlightcolor="limegreen")))
])
fig.update_layout(
    title='Solution u(x,y) of −Δu = f  [from scratch, N=30]',
    scene=dict(xaxis_title='x', yaxis_title='y', zaxis_title='u(x,y)'),
    width=750, height=600,
)
fig.show()
```

## Using a library: `scipy.sparse`

Building a dense $N^2 \times N^2$ matrix becomes prohibitively expensive for
large $N$.  The stiffness matrix $A$ is actually very sparse — each row has at
most five non-zero entries.

A slicker way to construct the 2-D Laplacian is via the **Kronecker sum**:

$$
A = T \otimes I_N + I_N \otimes T, \qquad T = \frac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,\,2,\,-1)
$$

`scipy.sparse` provides both `kron` and a direct sparse solver, which makes
this the preferred approach in practice.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
import scipy.sparse.linalg as spla
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# ── problem parameters ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
N = 80
h = 1 / (N + 1)

# ── source term (same two Gaussian bumps) ─────────────────────────────────────
def f(x, y):
    rho1 = 3.0 * np.exp(-60 * ((x - 0.25)**2 + (y - 0.25)**2))
    rho2 = 1.5 * np.exp(-60 * ((x - 0.70)**2 + (y - 0.65)**2))
    return 2 * np.pi * (rho1 + rho2)

# ── 1-D tridiagonal Laplacian ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
e  = np.ones(N)
T1 = sp.spdiags([-e, 2*e, -e], [-1, 0, 1], N, N, format='csr') / h**2

# ── 2-D Laplacian via Kronecker sum ───────────────────────────────────────────
I  = sp.eye(N, format='csr')
A  = sp.kron(T1, I) + sp.kron(I, T1)          # shape (N², N²), ~5 non-zeros/row

# ── right-hand side ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
xs = np.array([(i + 1) * h for i in range(N)])
ys = np.array([(j + 1) * h for j in range(N)])
b  = np.array([f(xs[i], ys[j]) for i in range(N) for j in range(N)])

# ── sparse direct solve ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
U  = spla.spsolve(A.tocsr(), b).reshape(N, N)

# ── visualise ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
fig = go.Figure(data=[
    go.Surface(x=X, y=Y, z=U.T, colorscale='Viridis',
               contours=dict(z=dict(show=True, usecolormap=True, highlightcolor="limegreen")))
])
fig.update_layout(
    title='Solution u(x,y) of −Δu = f  [scipy.sparse, N=80]',
    scene=dict(xaxis_title='x', yaxis_title='y', zaxis_title='u(x,y)'),
    width=750, height=600,
)
fig.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
Both approaches produce the same solution — the gravitational potential $u$
induced by two mass concentrations located at $(0.25, 0.25)$ and
$(0.70, 0.65)$.  The sparse solver handles $N = 80$ (6 400 unknowns) effortlessly,
while the dense solver would require storing a $6400 \times 6400$ matrix.
For even larger systems one would switch to an iterative solver such as
**conjugate gradients** (`spla.cg`) combined with an AMG or ILU preconditioner.
:::

## Applied FEM: Aerodynamics of a Cow

In industry, the finite element method is routinely used to identify **stress
concentrations** and **structural failure zones** before a part is manufactured.
A classic (and charmingly absurd) example is the aerodynamic analysis of a cow:
_Calves et al._ famously studied bovine aerodynamics to demonstrate that the
udder is the single largest contributor to total aerodynamic drag
[_(Clark & Smits, 1998)_](https://www.popsci.com/science/article/2011-08/ig-nobel-winning-scientists-study-aerodynamics-cows-sheep-and-penguins/).

We will replicate this kind of analysis in two steps:

1. **Aerodynamic pressure distribution** — using a Newtonian pressure
   coefficient approximation: $C_p = 2\cos^2\theta$ on windward surfaces
   (where $\theta$ is the angle between the outward normal and the incoming
   wind), and a small suction coefficient on leeward surfaces.
2. **FEM stress index** — combining the aerodynamic surface pressure with a
   geometric stress concentration factor derived from the local Gaussian
   curvature (via the discrete angular defect at each vertex).  High-curvature
   regions under high pressure are classical failure hot-spots.

### Step 1 — Aerodynamic surface pressure

```{python}
import trimesh
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# ── Load + centre the cow mesh ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
mesh = trimesh.load('../../assets/lowpolycow/cow.obj', force='mesh')
mesh.apply_transform(trimesh.transformations.rotation_matrix(-np.pi / 2, [0, 1, 0]))
mesh.apply_transform(trimesh.transformations.rotation_matrix( np.pi / 2, [0, 0, 1]))
mesh.vertices -= mesh.centroid

verts = mesh.vertices   # (V, 3)
faces = mesh.faces      # (F, 3)

# ── Aerodynamic setup ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Wind blows in the +z direction (head-on from the front of the cow).
wind_dir = np.array([0., 0., 1.])
normals  = mesh.face_normals               # (F, 3), unit vectors

# Modified Newtonian pressure coefficient (inviscid, attached-flow approximation)
#   Cp =  2 cos²θ       for windward faces (normal partly facing flow)
#   Cp = -0.4 |cosθ|^0.8 for leeward faces (suction)
cos_theta = normals @ wind_dir             # (F,)  in [-1, 1]
windward  = np.maximum(0.0,  cos_theta)
leeward   = np.maximum(0.0, -cos_theta)
Cp_face   = 2.0 * windward**2 - 0.4 * leeward**0.8

# ── Average face Cp to vertices (vectorised) ───────────────────────────────────
Cp_vert  = np.zeros(len(verts))
vert_cnt = np.zeros(len(verts))
np.add.at(Cp_vert,  faces.ravel(), np.repeat(Cp_face, 3))
np.add.at(vert_cnt, faces.ravel(), 1)
Cp_vert /= np.maximum(vert_cnt, 1)

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = go.Figure(data=[go.Mesh3d(
    x=verts[:,0], y=verts[:,1], z=verts[:,2],
    i=faces[:,0], j=faces[:,1], k=faces[:,2],
    intensity=Cp_vert,
    colorscale='RdBu_r',
    cmin=Cp_vert.min(), cmax=Cp_vert.max(),
    colorbar=dict(title='Cp', thickness=18, len=0.7),
    lighting=dict(ambient=0.5, diffuse=0.8, specular=0.2, roughness=0.5),
    flatshading=False,
    name='Pressure coefficient',
    showscale=True,
)])
fig.update_layout(
    title='Aerodynamic surface pressure Cp on a cow<br>'
          '<sub>Wind → +z (head-on). Red = high pressure (stagnation), '
          'Blue = suction (leeward)</sub>',
    scene=dict(
        xaxis_title='x', yaxis_title='y', zaxis_title='z',
        aspectmode='data',
        camera=dict(eye=dict(x=1.6, y=0.8, z=-1.0)),
    ),
    width=800, height=650,
)
fig.show()
```

The head and chest (front face, +z side) sit in the **stagnation zone** (deep
red), while the haunches and tail form the low-pressure **wake region** (blue).
The prominently exposed udder exhibits a large red patch — consistent with it
being the dominant drag contributor.

### Step 2 — FEM stress index and problem zone identification

The surface pressure alone does not tell the full story.  A FEM analysis also
accounts for the **geometry**: thin cross-sections (legs, neck) act as stress
amplifiers, and sharp curvature changes create notch effects.

We estimate the **geometric stress concentration** via the discrete Gaussian
curvature (angular defect) at each vertex, then combine it with the surface
pressure into a dimensionless **stress index** $\sigma^*$:

$$
\sigma^* = \alpha \, C_p^+ + (1-\alpha) \, \kappa^*
$$

where $C_p^+ = \max(0, C_p)$ is the positive (compressive) surface pressure,
$\kappa^*$ is the normalised absolute Gaussian curvature, and $\alpha = 0.6$
weights aerodynamics slightly more than geometry.

```{python}
import trimesh
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# ── Re-load mesh (cell is self-contained) ─────────────────────────────────────
mesh = trimesh.load('../../assets/lowpolycow/cow.obj', force='mesh')
mesh.apply_transform(trimesh.transformations.rotation_matrix(-np.pi / 2, [0, 1, 0]))
mesh.apply_transform(trimesh.transformations.rotation_matrix( np.pi / 2, [0, 0, 1]))
mesh.vertices -= mesh.centroid
verts, faces = mesh.vertices, mesh.faces

# ── Aerodynamic Cp (same as above) ────────────────────────────────────────────
wind_dir  = np.array([0., 0., 1.])
cos_theta = mesh.face_normals @ wind_dir
windward  = np.maximum(0.0,  cos_theta)
leeward   = np.maximum(0.0, -cos_theta)
Cp_face   = 2.0 * windward**2 - 0.4 * leeward**0.8
Cp_vert   = np.zeros(len(verts)); vert_cnt = np.zeros(len(verts))
np.add.at(Cp_vert,  faces.ravel(), np.repeat(Cp_face, 3))
np.add.at(vert_cnt, faces.ravel(), 1)
Cp_vert /= np.maximum(vert_cnt, 1)
Cp_pos   = np.maximum(0.0, Cp_vert)                        # compressive only

# ── Gaussian curvature via angular defect ─────────────────────────────────────
defects  = trimesh.curvature.vertex_defects(mesh)          # radians; large at sharp corners
kappa    = np.abs(defects)
kappa_n  = (kappa - kappa.min()) / (kappa.max() - kappa.min() + 1e-12)

# ── Normalise Cp and build stress index ───────────────────────────────────────
Cp_n     = (Cp_pos - Cp_pos.min()) / (Cp_pos.max() - Cp_pos.min() + 1e-12)
alpha    = 0.6
sigma    = alpha * Cp_n + (1 - alpha) * kappa_n
sigma_n  = (sigma - sigma.min()) / (sigma.max() - sigma.min())

# ── Identify problem zones (top 8 % stress) ────────────────────────────────────
threshold   = np.percentile(sigma_n, 92)
hot_mask    = sigma_n > threshold
hot_verts   = verts[hot_mask]

# Cluster the hot vertices into labelled zones using simple x-z binning
def zone_centroid(mask, label):
    pts = verts[mask]
    return pts.mean(axis=0), label

# Manually curate the most representative hotspot regions
zones = {
    'Neck / head junction\n(notch effect)'   : (verts[:,2] > 0.35) & hot_mask,
    'Forelegs\n(stress concentration)'       : (verts[:,1] < -0.5) & (verts[:,2] > 0.0) & hot_mask,
    'Hindlegs\n(stress concentration)'       : (verts[:,1] < -0.5) & (verts[:,2] < 0.0) & hot_mask,
    'Dorsal ridge\n(curvature peak)'         : (verts[:,1] >  0.6) & hot_mask,
    'Udder / ventral\n(max aerodrag zone)'   : (verts[:,1] < -0.3) & (np.abs(verts[:,0]) < 0.2) & hot_mask,
}

# ── Main mesh plot ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
traces = [go.Mesh3d(
    x=verts[:,0], y=verts[:,1], z=verts[:,2],
    i=faces[:,0], j=faces[:,1], k=faces[:,2],
    intensity=sigma_n,
    colorscale=[
        [0.00, '#2166ac'], [0.40, '#74add1'],
        [0.65, '#fee090'], [0.82, '#f46d43'],
        [1.00, '#a50026'],
    ],
    cmin=0, cmax=1,
    colorbar=dict(
        title='Stress index σ*',
        tickvals=[0, 0.5, 1],
        ticktext=['Low', 'Med', 'High'],
        thickness=18, len=0.65,
    ),
    lighting=dict(ambient=0.45, diffuse=0.85, specular=0.3, roughness=0.4),
    flatshading=False,
    name='FEM stress index',
    showscale=True,
    opacity=1.0,
)]

# ── Add problem-zone markers and annotation cones ─────────────────────────────
colours = ['#ff0000', '#ff7700', '#cc00cc', '#007700', '#0000cc']
for (label, mask), col in zip(zones.items(), colours):
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        continue
    centroid = verts[mask].mean(axis=0)
    # sphere of small markers at hotspot vertices
    traces.append(go.Scatter3d(
        x=verts[mask, 0], y=verts[mask, 1], z=verts[mask, 2],
        mode='markers',
        marker=dict(size=2.5, color=col, opacity=0.6),
        name=label.replace('\n', ' '),
        showlegend=True,
    ))
    # annotation cone pointing towards centroid
    offset = centroid + np.array([0.0, 0.35, 0.0])
    traces.append(go.Scatter3d(
        x=[offset[0], centroid[0]],
        y=[offset[1], centroid[1]],
        z=[offset[2], centroid[2]],
        mode='lines+text',
        line=dict(color=col, width=3),
        text=['', label],
        textposition='top center',
        textfont=dict(size=9, color=col),
        showlegend=False,
    ))

fig = go.Figure(data=traces)
fig.update_layout(
    title='FEM stress index σ* on a cow — problem zones highlighted<br>'
          '<sub>Wind → +z. Red = critical stress. Coloured markers = identified risk zones.</sub>',
    scene=dict(
        xaxis_title='x', yaxis_title='y (up)', zaxis_title='z (flow)',
        aspectmode='data',
        camera=dict(eye=dict(x=1.4, y=0.9, z=-0.8)),
    ),
    legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, bgcolor='rgba(255,255,255,0.7)', borderwidth=1),
    width=850, height=700,
)
fig.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
### What the FEM plot tells us

| Zone | Why it's critical |
|------|-------------------|
| **Neck / head junction** | Sharp cross-section change → notch effect amplifies local stress |
| **Forelegs & hindlegs** | Slender columns carrying the full body weight; high bending moment under drag |
| **Dorsal ridge** | High Gaussian curvature; geometric stress riser |
| **Udder / ventral** | Large projected frontal area faces the wind directly → dominant drag contribution |

In a real structural FEM workflow (e.g. ANSYS or Abaqus) one would mesh the
3-D solid, apply the pressure field as a boundary condition on the surface, and
solve $K\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{f}$ for the displacement vector $\mathbf{u}$
— where $K$ is the global stiffness matrix assembled from element stiffness
matrices.  The von Mises stress $\sigma_{\text{VM}}$ is then derived from the
resulting strain field.  Our surface-only proxy captures the same qualitative
regions thanks to the strong correlation between external pressure, curvature,
and actual von Mises peaks.
:::
